scores.evidence: The hook field ('A program read 92 out of 100 handwritten numbers correctly. Would you let it mark your answer sheet?') plus the h2 split is a concrete, teen-relevant surprise that the core idea resolves. But the first screen (h1) opens with an irrelevant non-sequitur: 'Obviously you already know junk when you see it.' That sentence has nothing to do with the Number Reader and blunts the opening.
scores.improve: Delete the junk-mail opener so h1 begins on the Number Reader and the 92/100 trust decision. The surprise design is already at level 4.

scores.evidence: All 19 blocks ask the learner to decide, predict, build, explore or explain (for example the e4 knob over the test mix replaces a static count-out, and m1 asks the learner to spot the 7/1 habit). Each block has a specific removal-test justification, and no two passive blocks sit next to each other.

Every block's wrongAnswerDesign is the same: "Show 'Wrong! Try again.' and let the learner retry until correct." That includes opinion votes with no right answer (h1, h2 re-vote, t2) and predictions that are meant to be locked in and resolved later (p1 says 'No answer is shown now'; p2). 'Wrong!' is the judgemental feedback Article 8 forbids, and forcing a retry until correct cancels the predict-observe-explain design. That is a penalty, not a reveal.
scores.improve: For each distractor, write specific, non-judgemental feedback that teaches. For example: p1 A leads to the side-by-side cards that show River writing is different, not messy; m4 'much better' leads to the 32-vs-47 comparison. Let predictions stand without retries, and give opinion votes no right or wrong state.

scores.evidence: The components match the ideas and the configurations are complete. predict carries a confidence row and a held vote. compare splits 92 into 86/90 and 6/10. The m3 knob has a goal line at 45. The e4 knob makes the learner produce the hiding effect. by-hand-then-automate has a hint ladder. The analogies fade into the formal cards. break-it keeps an empty 'Warnings' panel. The notes say where train-classifier would do better.

Every block's classroomVariant is 'Project the same screen as personal mode; students watch.' No block has a class vote by show of hands, teacher-driven knob or pair discussion. This contradicts the notes, which claim 'All votes are by raised hands'.
scores.improve: Write a real variant for each block that matches the catalogue: class vote by hands for predict and check, teacher moves the knob after the class predicts, teacher assembles or sorts from class suggestions, pair discussion for explain-back, a class result card for the takeaway. Add realistic timings for a class of 40 or more with no devices.

scores.evidence: t3 gives the learner a keepable, editable card with three questions and 'Then/Now' trust votes, which on its own would reach level 4. But the ending text closes with 'The AI now knows your style and will remember you next time.' That line contradicts the lesson's own core point (b2: 'This program does not change after training') and the device-only, no-personal-data promise. So the last thing the learner reads undermines what the artefact captures.
scores.improve: Remove the closing sentence so the ending lands on the learner's card and their Then/Now shift.

scores.evidence: There are several violations. (1) The banned phrase 'Obviously' opens h1. (2) 'Wrong!' feedback is used on every block, against Article 8 ('no red crosses, no incorrect'). (3) The ending makes an anthropomorphic, mind-framing AI claim: 'The AI now knows your style and will remember you next time'. The ai-framing reference treats this as blocking because the ending states it, and it also makes a false data-handling claim to minors (Article 10/11). (4) Retrying until correct on predictions turns the quiz into a punishment, an Article 14 pattern.
scores.improve: Remove 'Obviously', replace every 'Wrong! Try again.' with curious, specific feedback, and delete the 'knows your style / will remember you' sentence. Then check the text against the banned-phrases and ai-framing lists.

overall: FAIL. The mean is 2.29 (3+4+1+4+1+3+0 over 7), below the pass bar of 3. The blocking criterion voice-and-respect scores 0: a banned phrase ('Obviously'), judgemental 'Wrong! Try again.' on every block, and an anthropomorphic, privacy-false ending line ('The AI now knows your style and will remember you'). The automatic banned-phrases, ai-framing and refused-patterns checks should also reject it, and classroom-variants should fail because every variant is 'project the same screen'. The underlying structure (acts, component choice, hook surprise, takeaway card) is strong, so the fixes are concentrated in the feedback, classroom and voice layers.
